hints: Focus on the words evenly spaced time intervals. What do you think happens to the amount of antibiotic in the blood in the hours after you swallow a tablet?
Remember the body constantly breaks down and excretes drugs, so think about why topping up regularly keeps the level above the lethal dose for bacteria.
walkthrough:
**Think what happens to one dose**

Imagine you take one antibiotic tablet. It is absorbed into the blood, reaches a peak, then the liver breaks it down and the kidneys excrete it. So the concentration falls over time.

Think of it like this: dose in, level up, then level down as it is removed.

**See why timing matters**

If you wait too long before the next dose, the concentration drops below the level that kills bacteria. The bacteria can then survive and keep multiplying.

If you take the next dose at the right time, you top it back up before it falls too low.

**Pick the best reason**

The aim is not to increase slowly, it is to get up to the effective level quickly and then stay there. Even spacing keeps the blood concentration constantly at a lethal level until all the pathogens are killed.

options.A: We do not want a slow increase. We want to reach the lethal concentration quickly and then hold it there.
options.B: Correct. Regular top-ups replace antibiotic lost by metabolism and excretion, maintaining a continuously lethal concentration in the body.
options.C: Even spacing helps treatment work, but it does not stop mutations for resistance arising. Completing the full course is what reduces survival of bacteria.
options.D: Antibiotics do not select to kill resistant strains. Resistant strains survive antibiotics, while sensitive strains are killed.
